title: The Chalukyas and Rashtrakutas
description: Six centuries of the Deccan: the Chalukyas of Badami, the Rashtrakutas of Ellora and Manyakheta, and the Chalukyas of Kalyani, from a cliff fort in 543 to the kingdom's break-up in about 1189.
note: Rashtrakuta capitals before Manyakheta are not certain, so their early chapters are placed at Ellora. The Narmada pin marks the river, not a known battlefield. The Malwa pin is at Ujjain and stands for the Paramara kingdom. Badami, Aihole and Pattadakal lie within 20 km of each other.

steps.title: A fort on the red cliffs
steps.text: In 543 CE Pulakeshin I had an inscription cut into a cliff at Vatapi, today’s Badami, recording that he fortified the hill and performed the horse sacrifice (ashvamedha), a rite claimed by kings asserting supreme rule. The red sandstone gorge, guarded by a lake, became the capital of the Chalukyas, who would dominate the western Deccan for two centuries.
steps.today: Badami, Bagalkot district, Karnataka; the cliff inscription survives above the lake.

steps.title: Gods carved into the rock
steps.text: Under Kirtivarman I and his brother Mangalesha, the Chalukyas cut four cave temples into the Badami cliff: two for Vishnu, one for Shiva and one for the Jain teachers (Tirthankaras). An inscription in Cave 3, dated 578 CE, records its dedication to Vishnu by Mangalesha. Its great reliefs of Vishnu as the dwarf who strides across the worlds still survive.
steps.today: The Badami cave temples, protected by the Archaeological Survey of India.

steps.title: Harsha stopped at the Narmada
steps.text: Pulakeshin II won the throne from his uncle Mangalesha in a civil war, then pushed his kingdom north. On the Narmada his army stopped Harsha of Kannauj, the strongest king in the north. The river became the frontier between them. The exact site is not known, and the date is disputed, usually given between about 618 and 635 CE.
steps.today: The Narmada, the traditional line between north India and the Deccan.

steps.title: A poet’s praise at Aihole
steps.text: In 634 CE the Jain poet Ravikirti composed a Sanskrit eulogy (prashasti) of Pulakeshin II for the Meguti temple at Aihole. It lists the king’s conquests, including his victory over Harsha. It also names the poets Kalidasa and Bharavi, which helps historians date them. Aihole’s dozens of early temples show builders trying out the forms of the stone temple.
steps.today: Aihole, Bagalkot district, Karnataka; the inscription is still on the Meguti temple wall.

steps.title: The Pallavas take Vatapi
steps.text: Pulakeshin II fought the Pallavas of Kanchipuram for years. In about 641 the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang visited and described its people as proud and warlike. In 642 the Pallava king Narasimhavarman I took Vatapi and called himself its conqueror (Vatapikonda). Pulakeshin probably died in the fighting. His son Vikramaditya I recovered the capital by about 655.
steps.today: Badami; a Pallava inscription of Narasimhavarman I survives on a rock there.

steps.title: A queen’s temple at Pattadakal
steps.text: Vikramaditya II avenged his ancestors by taking Kanchipuram in about 740, but did not sack it; an inscription records his gifts to its Kailasanatha temple. To mark the victory, his queen Lokamahadevi built the Virupaksha temple at Pattadakal, where Chalukya kings were crowned. Its northern and southern temple styles side by side made Pattadakal a World Heritage Site.
steps.today: Pattadakal, Bagalkot district, Karnataka; a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.

steps.title: A feudatory overthrows his lords
steps.text: In about 753 Dantidurga, a Rashtrakuta chief who had served the Chalukyas, defeated Kirtivarman II and took the western Deccan. Where the Rashtrakutas came from is disputed. Dantidurga left an inscription in a cave at Ellora, a hillside already carved with Buddhist monasteries. The Chalukyas of Badami faded away, though a related branch lived on at Vengi.
steps.today: The Ellora Caves, near Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (Aurangabad), Maharashtra.

steps.title: A temple cut from one rock
steps.text: Dantidurga’s uncle and successor Krishna I is credited with the Kailasa temple at Ellora (Cave 16). Instead of building upward, workers cut down into the hillside, freeing a whole temple to Shiva, with courtyard, shrine and life-sized elephants, from one mass of basalt. A later Rashtrakuta grant praises it as a wonder. It is among the largest rock-cut monuments anywhere.
steps.today: The Ellora Caves, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983.

steps.title: Racing for Kannauj
steps.text: Kannauj, Harsha’s old capital, was the prize of north India, fought over by three powers: the Pratiharas of the west, the Palas of Bengal and the Rashtrakutas. Dhruva marched north and beat both rivals between the Ganga and the Yamuna. His son Govinda III came back, defeated the Pratihara Nagabhata II and claimed his horses drank from Himalayan streams.
steps.today: Kannauj, Uttar Pradesh, on the Ganga.

steps.title: Amoghavarsha’s capital
steps.text: Amoghavarsha I ruled for more than sixty years from Manyakheta. A patron of Jain scholars, he is credited with the Kavirajamarga, the oldest surviving work in Kannada, a guide to poetry, though some give it to his court poet Srivijaya. In about 851 the Arab merchant Sulaiman ranked the Rashtrakuta king among the four greatest rulers in the world.
steps.today: Malkhed, Kalaburagi district, Karnataka; little of the capital survives.

steps.title: Victory at Takkolam
steps.text: Krishna III, the last great Rashtrakuta, marched south against the rising Cholas. At Takkolam in 949 the Chola crown prince Rajaditya was killed on his elephant, struck down by Krishna’s ally the Ganga king Butuga II. Krishna held the Chola north around Kanchipuram for years, and his inscriptions claim conquests further south. It was the empire’s last high point.
steps.today: Takkolam, Ranipet district, Tamil Nadu, west of Chennai.

steps.title: Manyakheta burns
steps.text: Five years after Krishna III died, the Paramara king Siyaka of Malwa raided south and sacked Manyakheta in 972. The empire collapsed. The next year Tailapa II, a feudatory who claimed descent from the old Chalukyas, overthrew the last Rashtrakuta, Karka II. He later captured and executed the Paramara king Munja. The Chalukyas were back for two more centuries.
steps.today: Malkhed, Karnataka; Malwa is the plateau around Ujjain and Dhar in Madhya Pradesh.

steps.title: Attimabbe’s gift
steps.text: Attimabbe, the widow of a Chalukya general, was one of the great patrons of her age. She had the Jain temple called the Brahma Jinalaya built at Lakkundi in about 1007, and paid for a thousand copies of the Kannada poet Ponna’s Shantipurana. Under the Chalukyas of Kalyani the region filled with temples in dark stone, ever more richly carved.
steps.today: Lakkundi, Gadag district, Karnataka; the Brahma Jinalaya still stands.

steps.title: War with the Cholas
steps.text: Someshvara I made Kalyani his capital and spent his reign fighting the Cholas over Vengi and the Krishna–Tungabhadra lands. At Koppam in 1054 the Chola king Rajadhiraja was killed, and his brother Rajendra II was crowned on the battlefield; both sides claimed victory, and the site is disputed. In 1068 Someshvara, gravely ill, drowned himself in the Tungabhadra.

steps.title: Vikramaditya VI’s new era
steps.text: Vikramaditya VI pushed aside his elder brother, took the throne in 1076 and began a new count of years, the Chalukya-Vikrama era. He ruled for fifty years. The Kashmiri poet Bilhana wrote his life in verse, and at his court the jurist Vijnaneshvara wrote the Mitakshara, a commentary on law that later guided Hindu inheritance law across much of India.
steps.today: Basavakalyan, Karnataka; the Mitakshara was still applied in Indian courts into the 20th century.

steps.title: The end at Kalyani
steps.text: In about 1162 the Kalachuri Bijjala, a Chalukya feudatory, seized Kalyani. By tradition his minister was Basava (Basavanna), whose verses (vachanas) in plain Kannada taught devotion to Shiva and rejected caste; the Lingayats trace their origin to him. Someshvara IV briefly won Kalyani back, but by about 1189 the kingdom was split between the Yadavas, Hoysalas and Kakatiyas.
steps.today: Basavakalyan is named after Basava; Lingayats remain one of Karnataka’s largest communities.

items.name: Pulakeshin II
items.role: The greatest Chalukya king of Badami.
items.text: He won the throne in a civil war with his uncle, stopped Harsha at the Narmada and conquered the eastern coast at Vengi, which he gave to his brother, founding the Eastern Chalukyas. The Aihole inscription is the main record of his reign. He is thought to have died when the Pallavas took Vatapi in 642.

items.name: Lokamahadevi
items.role: Queen of Vikramaditya II and temple builder.
items.text: A princess of the Haihaya family and queen of Vikramaditya II, she built the Virupaksha temple at Pattadakal, first called Lokeshvara after her, to mark her husband’s victories over the Pallavas. Her sister Trailokyamahadevi, also his queen, built the Mallikarjuna temple beside it. The Virupaksha temple is still in worship.

items.name: Amoghavarsha I
items.role: Rashtrakuta king and patron of learning.
items.text: He came to the throne as a boy and ruled for more than sixty years, one of the longest reigns in Indian history. He faced revolts and wars with the Eastern Chalukyas, but is remembered for learning: the Jain scholar Jinasena taught at his court. Tradition says he gave up the throne late in life to follow Jain teaching.

items.name: Attimabbe
items.role: Jain patron under the Chalukyas of Kalyani.
items.text: The widow of the Chalukya commander Nagadeva, she was given the title ‘wish-granting gem of giving’ (Danachintamani) for her gifts to Jain temples and scholars. Kannada poets praised her, and inscriptions record her generosity. She is remembered as one of the great women patrons in the history of Karnataka.

items.name: Vikramaditya VI
items.role: The best-known king of the Chalukyas of Kalyani.
items.text: As a prince he fought the Cholas and married a Chola princess. As king he fought Chola and Hoysala rivals for Vengi and the south, and his long reign was the dynasty’s height. Bilhana’s Vikramankadevacharita tells his life. The Chalukya-Vikrama era he began was used in Deccan inscriptions for decades.
